name: Marine Drive
label: Marine Drive
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Pherozeshah Mehta Gardens' (4 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Sir Pherozeshah Mehta Road' (roads).
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-18: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).
notes: Curved seafront promenade known as the Queen's Necklace.

text.description:
Marine Drive is the 3-kilometre curved promenade along Mumbai's bay, known as the Queen's Necklace. The name comes from the streetlights, which look like a string of pearls when seen from above at night. The road and promenade were built in 1940, and the sweep of the bay and the palm-lined walkway make it easy to photograph. The wide concrete road follows the shoreline in a gentle banana shape. Behind it stand pale art deco apartment blocks. Some of the earliest, such as Kapur Mahal, Zaver Mahal and Keval Mahal, were built between 1937 and 1939 and belong to the UNESCO-listed Victorian Gothic and Art Deco Ensembles of Mumbai.

The best way to see the whole curve is from above. Pherozeshah Mehta Gardens, also called the Hanging Gardens, on Malabar Hill are the recommended elevated viewpoint. From the terraces you look back across the bay and see the full C-shaped arc, with the Arabian Sea beside it and the south Mumbai skyline behind. Go around sunset, when the streetlights start to come on and the curve begins to glow. If you would like a different angle, Kamala Nehru Park nearby gives a similar high view, and Girgaon Chowpatty shows the curve running away from the beach.

Keep your phone steady against a wall or railing, and take a few frames as the light changes.
text.geographic_location: Marine Drive runs along the bay in south Mumbai, between Nariman Point at the southern tip and Girgaon Chowpatty and Malabar Hill at the northern end.
text.directions_text: There are no railway or tram stops listed for this viewpoint. Start from Girgaon Chowpatty at the northern end of Marine Drive and take a short taxi ride up Malabar Hill to Pherozeshah Mehta Gardens (the Hanging Gardens). Ask the driver for the Hanging Gardens on Malabar Hill. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the whole curve of the bay and the sky. Then try the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pull the lines of streetlights and buildings closer together. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if a terrace railing or trees block the view, because it makes the distant curve look small.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Pherozeshah Mehta Gardens (Hanging Gardens terraces on the western ridge of Malabar Hill, looking back toward the bay). The whole C-shaped Marine Drive curve along the bay, with the Arabian Sea and the south Mumbai skyline behind it, often seen best at sunset. Stand on a terrace and look back across the bay towards Marine Drive.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the curve of the road along one of the lower lines, with the sea and sky filling the rest. Keep the horizon level. If you want a different view, Kamala Nehru Park has a high view with the Old Woman's Shoe structure in the foreground, and Girgaon Chowpatty shows the curve from beach level.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest part of the sky to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the lights stay sharp and don't glare. Once the streetlights are on, try night mode. Rest your elbows on a wall and hold still while it works. Take a few shots, because moving people and traffic can blur single frames.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset, as the streetlights come on. The sun's position along Marine Drive shifts through the year, so arrive early and watch how the light falls.

text.access_note: The Hanging Gardens is a public park, so check opening hours and any entry fee locally before you go.

name: Gateway of India
label: Gateway of India
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Statue Plaza' (2 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Shivaji Maharaj Statue' (pois).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/28845634: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Gateway of India' (57 m across).
notes: Waterfront basalt arch from 1924 and the city's best-known landmark.

text.description:
The Gateway of India is a tall basalt arch on Mumbai's waterfront, finished in 1924 and standing about 26 metres high. It was built to mark the 1911 landing of King George V, the first British monarch to visit India, and it later became the ceremonial exit for the last British troops in 1948. The design by George Wittet mixes Indo-Saracenic style with Gujarati details, so look for the fine stone latticework around the smaller arches and the four turrets above the central arch.

This avoids the dead-centre selfie view. The arch sits against the red dome of the Taj Mahal Palace hotel, and the statue on the plaza gives you something in the foreground. Guides say the raised plaza gives a slightly higher angle.

The area is busy with locals, vendors and other photographers, so be patient and wait for a gap. Security is tight here. Hold your phone in your hand rather than bringing a tripod, and don't fly a drone. If you want the arch framed symmetrically against the harbour, walk down to the Gateway itself. One guide suggests Apollo Bunder gives a wider harbour view that takes in the arch, the hotel and the boats, but verify this on the ground.
text.geographic_location: The Gateway of India stands on the Apollo Bunder waterfront in Mumbai, overlooking the Arabian Sea and Mumbai Harbour. It stands opposite the Taj Mahal Palace hotel.
text.directions_text: From there the Gateway is about 124 m to the south-east. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to get the arch and the hotel dome together. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the crowds push you close, but keep the arch away from the edges of the frame, where it can look stretched. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the latticework and the turrets.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Statue Plaza (left of the Gateway when facing the sea). The arch with the Taj Mahal Palace red dome beside it, with the statue adding a foreground element.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the arch on one third of the frame and the hotel dome on the other, with the statue low down as a foreground element. Keep the phone level so the arch doesn't lean. For a symmetrical view of the arch against the water, walk down to the Gateway itself. One guide suggests Apollo Bunder gives a wider harbour panorama, but verify this on the ground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the arch to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky and the hotel's red dome don't wash out. Take a few frames, because people keep walking through.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset, when the hotel facade catches warm light.

text.access_note: The Gateway stands in an open waterfront area, but security is tight and the upper levels and turrets are closed to the public, so check the official site before you go.

name: Taj Mahal Palace Hotel
label: Taj Mahal Palace
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Gateway of India' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Gateway of India - गेटवे ऑफ इंडिया' (way/28845634): middle (57 m across); moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/28846517: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Taj Mahal Palace' (211 m across).
notes: Historic domed hotel facing the Gateway of India.

text.description:
The Taj Mahal Palace is the grand old hotel beside the Gateway of India in Colaba. It opened on 16 December 1903 and was commissioned by Jamsetji Tata. Its Indo-Saracenic style, with a Moorish-looking dome and a long, detailed façade, gives it plenty to photograph. The best-known frame is from the harbour-facing plaza in front of the Gateway of India. From there the arch sits in the foreground, boats and open water lie beyond it, and the hotel dome rises beyond it to the west. The arch and the dome balance each other, so one picture shows two landmarks and the harbour setting.

The building has two parts: the original Palace of 1903 and the separate Tower, which opened in 1972. The Palace was once entered from the land-facing side, where the pool now is, so the harbour side you see from the plaza was not originally the main front. A second option is the Apollo Bandar Promenade, which shows the façade and domes straight on, with the Gateway also in the frame from the east. Check that name on the map before you rely on it.

The plaza is a security site, so keep your phone in your hand and work quickly and politely. Photos inside the hotel are reportedly limited to guests, so plan on exterior shots only.
text.geographic_location: In Colaba, at the southern end of Mumbai, right next to the Gateway of India and facing the harbour.
text.directions_text: No stations or tram stops are near this spot, so head for Colaba and the Gateway of India. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the arch, the water and the hotel dome in one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, more natural view. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details of the dome and façade.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Gateway of India (harbour-facing plaza in front of the arch, looking south-west toward the hotel). The arch in the foreground with harbour boats and water beyond, with the hotel's Moorish dome rising to the south. Moving a little nearer the jetty brings both landmarks into one shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the arch on one side and the hotel dome on the other, so they balance. Keep some water and boats in the lower part of the frame. For a straight-on view of the façade and domes, try the Apollo Bandar Promenade as an alternative, where the Gateway also appears in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the hotel to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky and floodlights keep their colour. After dark, use night mode and hold your phone steady against a wall or railing. Wide shots work better handheld than zoomed in.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunrise, for a quieter plaza and warm light on the arch. Blue hour is the other good moment, when the arch and hotel are both floodlit.

text.access_note: The Gateway of India plaza is an open public space with police and security presence, and the hotel is a private working hotel, so shoot its exterior from outside and check the official site before you go if you want to visit inside.

name: Haji Ali Dargah
label: Haji Ali Dargah
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Lala Lajpat Rai Marg' (2 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Lala Lajpat Rai Park' (pois).
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Haji Ali Dargah'.
notes: White mosque and tomb on an islet reached by a causeway.

text.description: Haji Ali Dargah is a white Sufi shrine on a small islet off Worli, in southern Mumbai, reached by a long, narrow causeway with the sea on both sides. The shrine holds the tomb of Pir Haji Ali Shah Bukhari, a merchant and saint from Bukhara, and dates from 1431. It is built in the Indo-Islamic style, and the islet sits roughly 500 metres from the shore. That makes it easy to photograph: a bright white building, open water around it and one clear line, the causeway, leading the eye straight to it. The best-known photo is taken from the mainland end of the walkway. Timing matters because the causeway can only be walked at low tide. It has no railings in places and goes under at high tide, when the shrine looks completely cut off. Thursdays and Fridays are the busiest days, as pilgrims come then, and on some Fridays there is Qawwali music. This is a working place of worship, so be discreet, keep your phone low near people at prayer, and stick to the causeway and exterior views. Photography inside the shrine is restricted and flash is not allowed.
text.geographic_location: On an islet in Haji Ali Bay, off the coast of Worli in southern Mumbai. The causeway starts on the mainland near the Mahalakshmi area.
text.directions_text: Head for the Mahalakshmi and Worli seafront and look for the start of the Haji Ali causeway on Lala Lajpat Rai Marg. Check the tide times first, because the causeway is only walkable at low tide. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to catch the whole causeway and the dargah in one frame. Switch to the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the white domes and minarets closer without walking out. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) once you are on the causeway, to get the sea on both sides and the sweep of the walkway.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Lala Lajpat Rai Marg (mainland end of the causeway, where the walk starts). The full length of the roughly 500-metre causeway running out to the white dargah on its islet, with the sea on both sides when the tide is medium.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the causeway on a vertical line so it leads the eye to the dargah, which sits near the top third of the frame. Keep the horizon level. For a different view, Worli Sea Face looks head-on across the bay at the dome and minarets, often with the Bandra-Worli Sea Link and the city skyline in the frame. If you walk out, keep to exterior and causeway shots, and ask permission if you are unsure about taking photos in the courtyard.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the white dargah to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the white walls keep their detail against the bright sky and water. A Live Photo can catch moving waves and people on the causeway. Don't use flash near the shrine.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Medium tide is best for this shot, as water is then visible on both sides of the causeway. The causeway is only walkable at low tide, so check tide times before you go.

text.access_note: This is a working place of worship, open to visitors of all faiths, but access depends on the tide and photography inside the shrine is restricted, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Telephoto zoom on a phone makes a distant building look closer and larger in the frame.
Reducing exposure on a phone helps keep detail in bright white surfaces.
Mahalakshmi and Worli are in the south of Mumbai, and the dargah lies to the north of the stand-here point.

name: Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus
label: CSMT Station
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation Building' (2 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation' (pois); moved 15 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/12176277888: the OpenStreetMap point 'Mumbai CSMT'.
notes: Gothic Revival railway station and UNESCO World Heritage Site.

text.description: Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus, still called CST, CSMT or simply VT by many Mumbai residents, is a working railway station and a UNESCO World Heritage Site. It was designed by Frederick William Stevens from an earlier sketch by Axel Haig, in an exuberant Gothic Revival style with Indian touches. Building began in 1878 and finished in 1887, and it opened to the public on 20 May 1888. It photographs well because the whole building is made for the eye: a tall ribbed central dome, turrets at the corners of the wings, and long rows of ornate windows. On top of the dome stands a figure of Progress holding a torch, which people often mistake for Queen Victoria. This spot gives you a quieter angle than the usual front-on shot. From the raised platform beside the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation Building, the station and the neighbouring BMC headquarters fit into one frame. It is a good place to show how the two grand buildings sit together. Expect heavy commuter crowds, and some views may be limited by building work at times. If you want the full Gothic front, D.N. Road gives it from the far pavement, with traffic in the foreground. Keep your phone steady against your body, take a few frames, and pick the one without people walking across the foreground.
text.geographic_location: In the Bori Bunder area of Mumbai, just south of where the old Bori Bunder station stood. The BMC headquarters is next door to the station.
text.directions_text: Ask for Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus (CSMT) by name. Head for the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation Building and find the raised platform beside it. From there the station is to the east, a short walk of roughly 3-4 minutes, and the platform gives a view toward it. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to get the station and the BMC building into one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched view of one building. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the dome, the turrets and the carved detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation Building (the raised platform beside the BMC building, next to the station). The station and the neighbouring BMC headquarters together in one frame, a quieter alternative to the main facade.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the station's dome on one of the upper intersections, with the BMC building filling the other side. Keep the phone level so the tall walls don't lean inwards. For a different view, D.N. Road shows the full Gothic front from the far pavement, and the street in front of the Times of India Building gives a head-on view of the main facade.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky doesn't wash out and the detail stays rich. Take a few frames in a row so you have one with no passers-by in the way.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Try to avoid commuter rush hours, roughly 8-10 AM and 5-8 PM, when the crowds are heaviest. Mid-morning after the rush or late in the afternoon is usually more comfortable and gives softer light.

text.access_note: The viewpoint is outside the station, but the building is a busy working railway terminus, so check the official site before you go for anything beyond the outside views.

name: Bombay High Court
label: Bombay High Court
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Oval Maidan' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Oval Maidan' (way/42352120): edge nearest the subject (712 m across).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q695852: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Neo-Gothic court building with a tall central tower.

text.description:
The Bombay High Court is one of the grandest Victorian buildings in Mumbai, and the view across the Oval Maidan is the classic way to see it. The open grass keeps the view clear, so the towers and the central part of the building are easy to see. The building is long, so the 0.5x lens may help if you want to fit more of it in.

The court was inaugurated in 1862. The present building was started in April 1871 and finished in November 1878, to a design by the British engineer Col. James A. Fuller. It is Gothic Revival in the Early English style, about 171 m long, with a tall central tower and two octagonal towers to the west. Statues of Justice and Mercy stand on top. It is part of the Victorian and Art Deco Ensemble of Mumbai, which became a World Heritage Site in 2018.

For a phone photo, the long, low building suits a wide, calm frame: path in the foreground, trees on both sides, towers at the end. Cricket is usually in progress on the ground, so keep clear of play and avoid close shots of people. If you want a second angle, Hutatma Chowk gives a street-level view of the facade with the Flora Fountain in front. Photography inside the court premises is restricted, so take your pictures from outside.
text.geographic_location: The High Court stands in south Mumbai, on the edge of the Oval Maidan and close to the Rajabai clock tower. Hutatma Chowk is opposite the High Court facade.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Oval Maidan in south Mumbai. Walk onto the open ground and stop at the centre, on the paved path, and look east. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the path, the trees and the towers with the central part of the building. Try 0.5x if you want to fit more of the long building, or 2x or 3x on the towers, if your phone has a telephoto lens, for a tighter frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Oval Maidan (centre of the ground, facing east along the paved path toward the Gothic buildings). The High Court's Gothic towers rise above the trees at the far end of the paved path across the open ground, with the Rajabai clock tower nearby. The view is open, with no cricket in the way.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and put the path on a line leading to the central tower, so the building sits level and centred. Keep the horizon straight, because tilted towers are very noticeable. For an alternative, Hutatma Chowk gives a street-level view of the facade across the square, with the Flora Fountain in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the towers to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky does not wash out and the stonework keeps its detail. Use 0.5x if you want to include more of the building, the ground and the sky, but keep the towers away from the edges of the frame, where they can look stretched.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people on the ground. In the afternoon the sun is behind you as you face east, so it should light the front of the building.

text.access_note: The Oval Maidan is a public ground, but its opening hours may have changed, and photography inside the court premises is restricted, so check the official site before you go.

name: Crawford Market
label: Crawford Market
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Lokmanya Tilak Marg' (4 web pages); placed at the stretch of Lokmanya Tilak Marg nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/49001325: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Crawford Market' (258 m across).
notes: Colonial-era market hall (Mahatma Jyotiba Phule Mandai).

text.description:
Crawford Market, officially the Mahatma Jyotiba Phule Mandai, is one of South Mumbai's best-known markets. Its Victorian Gothic building was finished in 1869 and given to the city by Cowasji Jehangir. It was first named after Arthur Crawford, the city's first Municipal Commissioner, and later renamed in honour of the social reformer Mahatma Jotirao Phule. The architect was William Emerson, who blended Victorian Gothic with Indian touches. The building is made of buff-coloured Kurla stone with redstone from Bassein. In 1882 it became the first building in India to be lit by electricity.

It photographs well because the clock tower rises above the busy street in front, so you get old stonework and city life in one frame. The entrance also has carved panels, two of them by John Lockwood Kipling, father of Rudyard Kipling. They are worth a close-up if you can get near.

For the classic view, shoot from the road on the clock-tower side, standing back far enough to fit the whole tower in. The pavement can be crowded and the traffic is heavy, so watch your step and keep a firm grip on your phone. Redevelopment work was reported to be under way as of 2025, so scaffolding may cover part of the facade. If you go inside, ask the vendors before photographing them and keep the flash off.
text.geographic_location: In South Mumbai, just north of Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus railway station and west of the JJ flyover, opposite the Mumbai Police headquarters. It stands at a busy road intersection.
text.directions_text: From the Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus area, the market is just to the north. You can get there by local train to Masjid Railway Station, by local bus or by cab. From there it is about 500 m on foot to the market building. Walk toward the market to the road in front of the clock-tower gate for the classic facade shot. Take care at the busy crossings. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Once you are on the road in front of the market, start with the default lens (1x) from across the street to fit the facade and clock tower. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you are close and the tower will not fit; keep the phone level, as it can make the building lean. Use 2x or more to pick out the clock tower or the carved panels.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Lokmanya Tilak Marg (clock-tower side of the market building, across the road from the facade). The Victorian Gothic facade with its clock tower rising above the busy street in front of the market. For the classic facade shot, walk toward the market to the road in front of the clock-tower gate and shoot from across the road, on the clock-tower side.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical line so the building stands straight. Step back along the pavement until the whole tower fits, and leave some street in the foreground to show the bustle. If the facade is partly covered by scaffolding, try a tighter 2x shot of the tower alone.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky does not wash out the stonework. Live Photos can catch the movement of traffic and people.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Earlier in the day is likely to be easier, as traffic is likely to build up later in the day.

text.access_note: The street view of the facade is from a public road.
claims_not_in_sources: Earlier in the day the street is likely to be less congested than later in the day.
An ultra-wide lens can make tall buildings appear to lean if the phone is tilted.

name: Flora Fountain
label: Flora Fountain
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Hutatma Chowk' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Hutatma Chowk' (way/130533404): middle (69 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/54224946: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Flora Fountain' (24 m across).

text.description:
Flora Fountain is an ornate stone fountain at the centre of Hutatma Chowk, the square at the southern end of Dadabhai Naoroji Road in the Fort district of South Mumbai. It was built in 1864 and shows the Roman goddess Flora, who tops the fountain. Four life-sized female figures at the corners carry foliage to stand for the four seasons. Richard Norman Shaw designed it and James Forsythe carved it in imported Portland stone. It stands where the old Church Gate of the Fort once stood.

It photographs well because the fountain sits in the middle of an open square with Victorian-era buildings around it, so you can show the monument and its setting in one picture. Beside it is the Martyr statue, added when the square was renamed Hutatma Chowk in 1960 to remember those who died in the struggle for Maharashtra State. Include it in the frame if you want the story of the place as well as the carving.

Face it from the lawn side and let the buildings fill the background. Keep the horizon straight and watch for people or traffic crossing the edge of the frame. Then move closer and shoot upwards for the figures and the carved detail. Traffic around the square is heavy, so stay on the pavement or the lawn and never step into the road for a shot.
text.geographic_location: Flora Fountain is in the Fort business district in the heart of South Mumbai. It stands in Hutatma Chowk, at the southern end of Dadabhai Naoroji Road.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Fort area of South Mumbai. Dadabhai Naoroji Road ends at the square, so if you are walking along it, keep heading south until you reach the fountain. Once you are the fountain is about 1 minute on foot to the south-west. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the fountain with the buildings behind it. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are too close to fit the square in. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the statues and carving.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Hutatma Chowk (in the middle of the square, facing the fountain from the lawn side). The fountain on its central base with the British-era Victorian buildings lining the square behind it, and the Martyr statue beside it if you include it in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the fountain on one of the vertical lines so the buildings fill the rest of the frame. Add the Martyr statue at one edge if you want it in the picture. For a different view, try the junction of Veer Nariman Road and Mahatma Gandhi Road, where the fountain stands among the Fort buildings, or Dadabhai Naoroji Road, where the High Court shows to one side of the fountain. Take care with traffic at both.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the fountain to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the pale stone keeps its detail against the bright sky. If the lights are on in the evening, try night mode and hold the phone still against your body.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is quieter, and one guide suggests 7:00-9:00 AM. Evening light from about 5:30-7:00 PM is another option, and the fountain looks striking when the lights come on.

text.access_note: The fountain stands in an open public square, but it was restored in 2017-2019 and may be fenced or closed for works, so check before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Traffic around the junction and square is heavy, so it is safer to stand on the pavement or the lawn.
The pale stone can lose detail against a bright sky, so lowering the exposure slider helps.
Night mode works best if the phone is held steady.

name: Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Vastu Sangrahalaya
label: Prince of Wales Museum
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Mahatma Gandhi Road' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Mahatma Gandhi Road nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/206808196: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Vastu Sangrahalaya' (96 m across).
notes: Indo-Saracenic museum building in Kala Ghoda.

text.description:
This is the big Indo-Saracenic museum in the heart of South Mumbai, once called the Prince of Wales Museum of Western India and renamed in 1998 after Shivaji. It was built to mark a royal visit, and the building was completed in 1915. It opened as a museum in 1922. The architect, George Wittet, also designed the Gateway of India. The walls are grey and buff local stone, topped by a central dome tiled in white and blue. Wittet modelled the dome on the one at Golconda Fort. Palm trees and flower beds surround the building, which gives you several different pictures.

The recommended viewpoint is the pavement of Mahatma Gandhi Road opposite the main gate. The frame here is the street view: the gate, its pillars and the entrance, with the museum behind and to the east. It is a good 'I was here' shot, and it is easy to reach on foot from Kala Ghoda. For the full facade with the dome and minarets, step into the gardens and use the lawn and palms as a frame. A newer steel visitor centre at the entrance may creep into some shots, so move a step or two to leave it out. Photography rules inside the museum vary, so check them on arrival.
text.geographic_location: In South Mumbai, on Mahatma Gandhi Road, close to the Gateway of India and within walking distance of Kala Ghoda.
text.directions_text: There is no station or tram stop right at this spot, so head for Kala Ghoda in South Mumbai. From there it is an easy walk along Mahatma Gandhi Road to the museum's main gate. The recommended viewpoint is the pavement opposite the main gate. The building lies to the east of it. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the gate and entrance from the pavement. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) inside the gardens, where you are closer to the building and want the whole facade. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the dome and the small domed pinnacles.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Mahatma Gandhi Road (pavement directly opposite the main gate). The main gate with its pillars and security entrance, seen from the street in a street-level frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the gate centred and the verticals straight. Hold the phone level so the pillars don't lean. For a second picture, go into the gardens and frame the facade between the palms, with the lawn in front and the white dome above. The Buddha statue works as a foreground in the garden view.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the gate to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the pale dome and sky don't turn white. If people walk through the frame, take a few shots or use a Live Photo and pick the cleanest one.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: No best time is recommended for this spot. As general light advice, softer daylight earlier or later in the day is usually kinder to stonework than harsh midday sun.

text.access_note: The pavement and gardens are outdoors, but entry to the museum grounds and interior photography rules can differ, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Softer daylight earlier or later in the day is kinder to stonework than harsh midday sun (general light advice).
People walking past on the pavement may enter the frame.

name: Rajabai Clock Tower
label: Rajabai Clock Tower
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Oval Maidan' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Oval Maidan' (way/42352120): edge nearest the subject (712 m across).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q7285587: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Gothic clock tower at the University of Mumbai.

text.description:
Rajabai Clock Tower rises 85 m above the Fort campus of the University of Mumbai, and its tall, carved outline suits a phone photo well. It was designed by the English architect Sir George Gilbert Scott, who modelled it on Big Ben in London. The foundation stone was laid in 1869 and the building was finished in November 1878. Its style mixes Venetian and Gothic, and it is built from buff-coloured Kurla stone, which looks warm and golden in good light. The tower is part of the Victorian and Art Deco Ensemble of Mumbai, which became a World Heritage Site in 2018. When it was built it was the tallest structure in the city, and it still chimes one tune every 15 minutes.

The best view is from the middle of the Oval Maidan, looking across to the tower. From there the whole height of the tower fits into one frame, with green grass below it and often cricketers in the foreground. The road between the Oval Maidan and the tower is busy, so take care if you cross. If you want a different angle, Karmaveer Bhaurao Patil Marg gives a street-level view looking up at the carved façade, with the university buildings around it. Keep the phone level so the tower does not lean, and leave a little space above the top so the finial is not cut off.
text.geographic_location: The tower is in the Fort area of south Mumbai, inside the Fort campus of the University of Mumbai. The Oval Maidan, the open ground used for this view, lies just across the road.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Fort area of south Mumbai and ask for the Oval Maidan. Go to the middle of the open ground and look east to find the tower. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the full height of the tower, the grass and any cricketers into one frame. Use the default lens (1x) for a tidier, less stretched view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the clock face and the carved stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Oval Maidan (middle of the ground, facing the tower). The full height of the tower framed over green grass, with cricketers in the foreground. For a second view, try Karmaveer Bhaurao Patil Marg, looking up at the façade from street level.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical grid line so it stands straight. Leave the grass in the lower third of the frame and let the tower fill the upper part. If you use the street-level view on Karmaveer Bhaurao Patil Marg, step back as far as is safe and tilt the phone up only slightly.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the tower to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky stays blue and the stone keeps its colour. Try a Live Photo to catch the cricketers moving. Keep clear of the traffic when you take pictures near the road.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon or sunset for golden light on the Gothic façade, or early morning for soft light and fewer people.

text.access_note: You photograph the tower from outside, and the interior is closed to the public; rules about taking photos close to the base may change, so check the official site and any signs before you go.

name: Bandra Fort
label: Bandra Fort
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Bandra Fort' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q5049681: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Portuguese ruin with views of the Sea Link.

text.description: Bandra Fort, also called Castella de Aguada, is a Portuguese fort on the headland at Land's End in Bandra. The Portuguese built it in 1640 as a watchtower looking over Mahim Bay and the Arabian Sea. It steps down over several levels, from the water's edge up to about 24 metres. That makes it a good place for photos with depth: old stone walls and ramparts in the foreground, open water behind them, and the Bandra-Worli Sea Link across the bay. The fort has appeared in Hindi films such as Dil Chahta Hai, so it may look familiar. It reopened in October 2024 after another round of restoration, so the walls may look more freshly finished than you expect. The best view of the bridge is from the far, western end of the rampart, where the fort juts out towards the sea. Walk out along the wall rather than shooting from the entrance. Keep your shots simple: let the wall lead the eye towards the water and the bridge. If you have time, Lands End Garden nearby gives a different view across Mahim Bay to the same bridge, with greenery in the foreground. Rocky surfaces can be slippery in the monsoon, so watch your footing while you hold your phone up. There is no shop or restroom at the fort.
text.geographic_location: Bandra Fort is at Land's End in Bandra, Mumbai, overlooking Mahim Bay and the Arabian Sea. The Taj Land's End hotel is nearby.
text.directions_text: There is no Underground, train or tram stop at this spot, so head for Bandra and then on to Land's End, using a map app if it helps. Look for Bandra Fort at Land's End. The fort is at the sea-facing western end of the Bandra headland. Once inside, walk to the far western end of the rampart, where the phone icon on the map is. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the rampart, the water and the bridge in one frame. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the old wall in the foreground. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the Bandra-Worli Sea Link closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here you look across the water to the Bandra-Worli Sea Link, with the Arabian Sea and the fort walls in front of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the rampart along the bottom third of the frame so the wall leads the eye towards the bridge. Keep the horizon level. For a different view, Lands End Garden nearby looks across Mahim Bay to the same bridge, with greenery in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bridge or the sky to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sunset colours do not turn white. Take a short Live Photo as well, in case the waves or people moving give a better moment. Hold the phone with both hands near the wall edge, and take care on wet rock.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Golden hour, just before sunset, when the old walls make a strong foreground. Opening times can vary, so check them before you go and allow time to get out to the far end.

text.access_note: The fort is owned by the Archaeological Survey of India; opening hours can vary and drone use is restricted without permission, so check the official site before you go.

name: Basilica of Our Lady of the Mount
label: Mount Mary Church
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Our Lady of Fatima Oratory' (2 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Oratory of Our Lady of Fatima' (pois).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/281241933: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Mount Mary Church' (70 m across).
notes: Hilltop basilica in Bandra overlooking the sea.

text.description:
The Basilica of Our Lady of the Mount, also called Mount Mary Church, sits on a small hill in Bandra with the Arabian Sea beyond it. The hill is about 80 metres above sea level, and that height gives the church its setting. Its twin spires rise above the trees and the neighbouring rooftops.

The present building is only about a hundred years old. The church on this spot was destroyed in 1738 during the Maratha attack on Bassein and was rebuilt in the British Bombay era. The statue of Mary inside goes back much further. Jesuit priests brought a statue here in the 16th century, and local Koli fisherfolk still call it Mot Maoli, the 'Pearl Mother'.

The best photo is from across the road, at Our Lady of Fatima Oratory. From there you can fit the spires into one frame and use the oratory's steps and the grotto as a foreground. The Mount Mary Stairs are a good second choice. From the foot or middle of the climb you see the facade and both spires, with the sea and the Bandra skyline opening out behind you.

The church gets very busy around the Bandra Fest on 8 September and the fair that follows, and Sundays can also be crowded. Outdoor photos are fine, but keep your phone away inside the church and during mass. Give people at prayer plenty of space.
text.geographic_location: In Bandra, on a hillock overlooking the Arabian Sea. The church sits at the top of the hill, with the Mount Mary Stairs climbing up to it.
text.directions_text: Head to Mount Mary Church on the hill in Bandra. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to get the whole church and the oratory's steps in one frame. Switch to telephoto (2x or 3x, depending on your phone) to pick out the two spires and cut out traffic and wires. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you stand close to the steps and the grotto and want them large in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Our Lady of Fatima Oratory (opposite side of the road from the main church entrance, near the Grotto). The church spires framed from across the road, with the oratory's steps and grotto in the foreground. The church is to the east of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put the oratory steps or the grotto in the lower part of the frame and let the spires rise above them. Turn on gridlines and line a spire up with a vertical line so the tower does not lean. Keep the phone level rather than tilting it up, and step back if the spires start to look squeezed. For a different view, climb the Mount Mary Stairs and shoot the facade with the sea and the Bandra skyline behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the church to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky does not turn pale and washed out. Take a few frames, because passers-by often walk through the shot. If someone is praying in the frame, wait or choose another angle.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon is usually calmer and gives softer light. Sundays and the Bandra Fest in early September are very crowded, so a weekday visit makes shooting easier.

text.access_note: This is a place of worship that is open to visitors. Photography is allowed outdoors but not inside the church, and it is restricted during mass, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people than midday.
Weekday visits are generally quieter than Sundays.
A telephoto lens (2x or 3x) helps isolate the spires from traffic and wires across the road.

name: St. Thomas Cathedral, Mumbai
label: St. Thomas Cathedral
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Horniman Circle Garden' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Horniman Circle Garden' (way/40743182): middle (170 m across); moved 10 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/158253023: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'St Thomas Cathedral' (62 m across).
notes: Oldest surviving British-built church in the city.

text.description:
St. Thomas Cathedral is the oldest church in Mumbai, and it sits in the old Fort area right beside Horniman Circle. Its foundation stone was laid in 1676, but the building was only opened for worship on Christmas Day 1718. It became a cathedral in 1837, and the tower and clock were added the following year. The name of Churchgate station comes from the gate in the old fort wall that once led to this church. The cathedral is also treated as the 'zero point' of colonial Bombay, from which milestones were laid out northwards.

It photographs well because the tall tower and rose windows rise above the surrounding Fort buildings, and from Horniman Circle Garden the greenery gives you a natural foreground. Walk over to the garden and look up at the tower, which is the classic view of the church. For a second angle, Veer Nariman Road looks straight at the front facade with the old buildings across the street. This road was once called Churchgate Street and led to the church gate.

The church is still in regular use, so be discreet, avoid flash and keep clear of services. Take your wide shots from the garden and save any close-ups for a quiet moment.
text.geographic_location: In the Fort area of South Mumbai, next to Horniman Circle, not far from Flora Fountain. The cathedral stands across the road from Horniman Circle Garden.
text.directions_text: Head for Horniman Circle in South Mumbai's Fort area and ask for St. Thomas Cathedral. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole tower and some garden greenery into one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the tower and rose windows.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Horniman Circle Garden (opposite the cathedral, on its east side across the road). The cathedral's tall tower and rose windows rising above the surrounding Fort buildings, with the garden greenery in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the tower on one of the vertical lines. Let the garden's trees and greenery fill the bottom of the frame. Tilt the phone upwards slightly, but keep the tower upright rather than leaning. If you want the front facade instead, try Veer Nariman Road, which looks straight at the church.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tower to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky does not wash out the stonework. If people are walking through, take a short burst or a Live Photo and pick the cleanest frame. Turn the flash off.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go in daylight. Avoid service times and Sunday prayers.

text.access_note: This is an active place of worship in a public part of the city; entry is reported to be free, but opening hours vary between guides, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Opening hours differ between guides, so they should be checked before a visit.
Photography inside is generally allowed but flash should be avoided and visitors should be discreet during services.

name: Banganga Tank
label: Banganga Tank
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Walkeshwar Road' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Walkeshwar Road nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/38718204: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Banganga Tank' (132 m across).
notes: Ancient sacred water tank among temples on Malabar Hill.

text.description: Banganga Tank is a rectangular temple tank in the Malabar Hill area, part of the Walkeshwar Temple complex. Steps run down on all four sides, and temples, shrines and old residential buildings sit around the rim, so the setting feels like a small village inside the city. The tank was built in AD 1127 by Lakshman Prabhu, a minister at the court of the Silhara kings of Thane, and was rebuilt in 1715. It is spring-fed, so the water stays sweet even though the sea is only a few dozen metres away. Local legend says it appeared when Lakshmana shot an arrow into the ground to fetch water for his brother Rama. For a phone photo, the approach lane and entrance street are a good place to start. From there you can frame the lane with its temple-lined edges and everyday street life, which gives a quieter and more personal picture than the steps. The tank itself is nearby, a few minutes on foot to the north-west, if you want the stepped banks, the shrines and reflections in still water. The water can look green and ritual offerings can make the edges untidy, so choose your framing with care. If people are taking part in a ceremony, ask permission before photographing them. In November, during Dev Diwali, large crowds light lamps around the tank.
text.geographic_location: Banganga Tank is on Malabar Hill in south Mumbai, within the Walkeshwar Temple complex and a short walk from the sea. The place to shoot is the approach lane and entrance street, so confirm the exact spot on the ground.
text.directions_text: From there, the tank is to the north-west, about 3 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the lane and its street life. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the lane feels tight, and use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for details of the temples and shrines without walking up to people.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Walkeshwar Road (the street at the entrance to the tank, where the approach lane meets the tank). The lane leading down to the tank, with everyday street life and the temple-lined approach in the frame. The place to shoot is the approach lane and entrance street, so confirm the exact spot on the ground. The tank lies to the north-west, so do not count on it appearing in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Use the lane as a leading line, with the temples and buildings on either side. Turn on gridlines to keep the buildings upright. For a different view, walk the short way north-west to the tank's own steps for the stepped banks, the shrines on the rim and reflections in the water. Keep the green water and offerings out of the frame by choosing your angle carefully.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the lane to set focus, then slide the exposure down slightly if the sky or white temple walls look washed out. Ask before photographing people, especially during ceremonies.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and a more relaxed lane. In November, Dev Diwali brings big crowds and many lamps around the tank.

text.access_note: This is a working temple complex, so treat it as a place of worship and be respectful of people at prayer.

name: Hanging Gardens of Mumbai
label: Hanging Gardens
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Kamala Nehru Park' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Kamala Nehru Park' (way/39181022): middle (311 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/38883141: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Pherozeshah Mehta Gardens (Hanging Gardens)' (323 m across).
notes: Terraced garden on Malabar Hill with city views.

text.description:
The Hanging Gardens are a set of terraced gardens on the western side of Malabar Hill, laid out in 1881 over the city's main reservoir. They are best known for hedges clipped into animal shapes and for sunset views over the Arabian Sea. They also go by the name Pherozeshah Mehta Gardens. Seen from the air, the paths spell out the letters PMG in cursive, but you will not see that from the ground.

The best phone photo here is taken from the other side of the road, in Kamala Nehru Park. The giant shoe-shaped Old Woman's Shoe structure makes a cheerful foreground. With the sea and the curve of Marine Drive behind it, you get a picture that says 'Mumbai' without needing a caption. It works especially well with children beside the shoe. Once you have that shot, cross over to the Hanging Gardens themselves. From there you can frame the curve of Marine Drive and the sea behind the animal-shaped hedges, ideally with the sun going down over the water.

Keep your shots simple. Use the default lens (1x) for the shoe and a little sea, and the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the terraces and hedges. Turn on gridlines to keep the horizon level. Wipe your lens before you start, as sea air can leave a haze on it. Expect other visitors in your frame at busy times, so wait a moment for a gap rather than editing people out later.
text.geographic_location: On the western side of Malabar Hill, in south Mumbai. The Hanging Gardens sit directly opposite Kamala Nehru Park.
text.directions_text: There is no station or tram stop at this spot, so head for Malabar Hill by taxi (or a local train plus auto) and ask for Kamala Nehru Park. Parking can be difficult, so a taxi is the easier choice. The Hanging Gardens are directly opposite the park. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the Old Woman's Shoe with the sea behind it. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) in the gardens to fit in the terraces and hedges. Try telephoto (2x or more) to pull the curve of Marine Drive closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Kamala Nehru Park (opposite the Hanging Gardens, next to the Old Woman's Shoe structure). The giant shoe-shaped Old Woman's Shoe structure, framed with the sea and Marine Drive in the background. The photo here shows the giant shoe with the sea and Marine Drive behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Keep the shoe large in the lower part of the frame and let the sea and the Marine Drive curve fill the background. Switch on gridlines and set the horizon on a grid line. As an alternative, cross to the Hanging Gardens and shoot the Queen's Necklace curve of Marine Drive over the animal-shaped hedges.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the shoe to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky and sea keep their colour. In portrait mode, children standing by the shoe will look sharper against the background.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon into sunset, when the sun goes down over the sea. Weekends and evenings are crowded, so a weekday visit or an earlier slot gives you a clearer view.

text.access_note: Both are public parks, but entry rules and opening times can change, so check the official site before you go.

name: Mani Bhavan
label: Mani Bhavan
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/39835569: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Mani Bhavan' (30 m across).
notes: House where Gandhi stayed, now a museum.

text.description: Mani Bhavan is a museum in a former mansion on Laburnum Road, in the Gamdevi part of Mumbai. It was Gandhi's Mumbai base from 1917 to 1934, and the house belonged to his friend and host Revashankar Jagjeevan Jhaveri. From here Gandhi launched several of his best-known campaigns, and it was while staying here that he took up the charkha, the spinning wheel. In 1955 the building was taken over by the Gandhi Smarak Nidhi to keep it as a memorial. Inside, there is a library with a statue of Gandhi, a staircase lined with pictures of his life, a photo gallery, and his own room on the second floor, where you can see two spinning wheels, a book and his bed through a glass partition. The terrace where he was arrested on 4 January 1932 also remains. It photographs well because it is a historic house on Laburnum Road, so the frame is about character rather than grandeur. Start with the building from the street, then look for details: the entrance, the windows and the way the house sits in its surroundings. A phone copes well with this kind of subject if you keep the lines straight and the exposure even. Inside, photography may be limited, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: Mani Bhavan is on Laburnum Road in the Gamdevi area of Mumbai.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from the Gamdevi area and use a taxi or a hired scooter to reach Laburnum Road. Ask your driver for Mani Bhavan on Laburnum Road, or show the address on a map. The phone icon on the map is right at the building, so there is no further walk once you arrive. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the front of the building as it looks to the eye. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you cannot fit the whole building in from where you stand, and keep the phone level to avoid leaning walls. Use telephoto (2x or more) for details such as the doorway or windows.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Take a step or two back along the street if you want the whole front in view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the vertical edges of the house up with them. Include a little of the street or any greenery at the edge of the frame for a sense of place. Take one wide shot, then move closer for a detail shot of the entrance or a window.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then slide the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the walls keep their colour and detail. If you go inside where photography is allowed, tap on the subject again, as the light will be lower.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daytime, when the street is well lit and you can see the building clearly. Early in the day is usually quieter on a city street.

text.access_note: Mani Bhavan is a museum, so opening arrangements and any photography rules may apply: check the official site before you go.

name: Bandra–Worli Sea Link
label: Bandra-Worli Sea Link
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Bandra Fort' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Bandra Fort' (way/39490158): middle (207 m across).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q314572: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.

text.description:
The Bandra–Worli Sea Link, officially the Rajiv Gandhi Sea Link, is a cable-stayed bridge that carries eight lanes of traffic across Mahim Bay, joining Bandra in the Western Suburbs to Worli in South Mumbai. It is 5.6 km long, and its tallest diamond-shaped concrete towers rise 128 metres. It was the first cable-stayed bridge built in open seas in India. Four lanes opened on 30 June 2009 and all eight were running by 24 March 2010.

It photographs well because the whole structure reads clearly from a distance. You see the towers, the fan of cables and the long curve of the deck against open water. The Land's End end of Bandra Fort faces the northern cable-stayed section, and several travel guides name it as the classic free view of the bridge, especially around sunset.

Keep the bridge as the main subject and use the fort wall or the sea as a simple foreground. Stopping or photographing on the bridge itself is prohibited, so shoot from the shore only. Reviews of the fort are mixed, with one calling it dirty and crowded, so be ready to wait a moment for a clear spot. Bandstand Promenade is a good alternative for a closer view of the bridge's northern end, but the rocks there can be unstable, so take care.
text.geographic_location: The viewpoint is Bandra Fort at Land's End, on the Bandra seafront in Mumbai's Western Suburbs. The bridge crosses Mahim Bay from Bandra south to Worli.
text.directions_text: Head for Bandra, then to Bandra station. Visitors reach the fort from there on foot or by local transport. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the whole bridge with the sea and sky around it. Then try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the cable-stayed span and the skyline behind it closer together. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a close foreground, because it makes the bridge look small and far away.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Bandra Fort (Land's End end of the fort, facing the bridge's northern cable-stayed section). The bridge's cable-stayed span rising from the Bandra side against the Arabian Sea, with the skyline behind. Stay on the shore and do not stop on the bridge itself.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the deck up with a horizontal line so the bridge looks level. Place the towers off-centre and leave open sea in the foreground. Include a piece of fort wall at the edge of the frame for depth. If you have time, Bandstand Promenade gives a view of the bridge's northern end with rocks and the Bandra coastline in front, and Worli Fort shows the whole span from the Worli side. Check access at Worli Fort before you go.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bridge to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sunset sky keeps its colour. After the sun has gone, try night mode and brace your elbows on the wall to keep the phone steady. Take a few frames, as people and boats come and go.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Around sunset, as the guides suggest.

text.access_note: Bandra Fort is described as a free public viewpoint, but opening hours and closures were not verified, so check locally before going; stopping or photographing on the bridge itself is prohibited.
claims_not_in_sources: At sunset the sun sets in the west over the sea, so the bridge may be partly backlit from Bandra Fort.
Telephoto (2x-5x) helps bring the span closer because the bridge is under a kilometre from the viewpoint.
Tapping to focus and lowering the exposure slider helps keep sunset skies from washing out.
Ultra-wide (0.5x) makes a distant subject look smaller.
Bracing your elbows on a wall helps keep the phone steady in night mode.

text.description: Girgaum Chowpatty is a public beach on the Girgaum waterfront, at one end of the Queen's Necklace, the long curve of Marine Drive, and right next to Malabar Hill. It photographs well because of that curve: the shoreline sweeps away in a graceful arc, and on a clear day the high-rises of Nariman Point stand at the far end. The sea faces west, so the beach is a classic place to watch the sun go down. The sand and water are a different matter. The sea here is polluted and not suitable for swimming, so treat the beach as a place to look and photograph rather than paddle. Kamla Nehru Park is nearby. From the higher ground on this side you look down over the beach and the Marine Drive curve, with the Nariman Point towers beyond. It is a quieter, higher alternative to the sand, and a place with unobstructed night views. The beach itself is very crowded at sunset and during Ganesh Visarjan, so if you want a clear frame of the crowd, shoot from above rather than pushing through it. Another option is the Girgaon Chowpatty Viewing Deck, which gives a side view looking south along the coast. Its current condition is uncertain, so check locally before you rely on it.
text.geographic_location: Girgaum Chowpatty is in the Girgaum area of south Mumbai, on the seafront beside Malabar Hill, at one end of the Queen's Necklace curve of Marine Drive.
text.directions_text: No railway or tram stops are listed for this spot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole beach and Marine Drive curve into one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view of the bay. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the Nariman Point towers or the sunset over the sea.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Kamla Nehru Park (Malabar Hill side, overlooking the beach). An aerial, wide-angle view of Chowpatty beach and the Marine Drive curve, with the Nariman Point towers beyond.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the curve of the coast along a diagonal line, with the towers in the upper third. Keep the horizon level. If you want to try a different angle, the Girgaon Chowpatty Viewing Deck offers a side view looking south, with the Queen's Necklace curving away.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the sky or the sea to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so sunset colours are not washed out. After dark, use night mode and rest your phone on a wall or railing to keep it steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon into sunset for the sea and sky, then stay on into dusk and see how the view looks after dark. The beach is at its most crowded at sunset.

text.access_note: The beach is a public space, but entry details and opening status for Kamla Nehru Park and the viewing deck may vary, so check locally before you go.

label: Dhobi Ghat
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q5269642: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Huge open-air laundry seen from the nearby bridge.

text.description:
Dhobi Ghat is an open-air laundry in the Mahalaxmi area of Mumbai, built in 1890. Rows of concrete wash pens sit side by side, each with its own flogging stone, and the washers (the dhobis) scrub, rinse and wring clothes and linens from the city's hotels and hospitals. It is claimed to be the world's largest outdoor laundry, and it is a popular stop for visitors from abroad.

It photographs well because of its pattern and colour. The grid of pens, the lines of cloth drying on ropes and the people working at each stone give you a busy scene with a clear structure. Around 7,000 people work here, often for 18 to 20 hours a day, and over 100,000 items are washed daily. Around 200 families live here, and the work has been passed down through generations.

For a phone, think wide first. Start with the whole view of the pens, then look for smaller scenes: a row of drying cloth, or one washer at a stone. Keep the horizon level, because the straight rows of pens look best when they are square to the frame. This is a place where people live and work, so photograph the scene rather than pushing a lens into anyone's face, and ask before taking close portraits.
text.geographic_location: Dhobi Ghat is in Mahalaxmi, in southern Mumbai, next to Mahalaxmi railway station and close to the Saat Rasta roundabout.
text.directions_text: Head for the Mahalaxmi area in southern Mumbai, near the Saat Rasta roundabout. You can reach it from Mahalaxmi railway station (Western Railway), Mahalaxmi Metro Station (Aqua Line) or Jacob Circle monorail station. Go to the phone icon on the map. From there the laundry is 123 m to the north-east, about 2 minutes on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 120 m south-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the full spread of pens, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as a single row of drying cloth or one washer at work.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 120 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east. Take your first wide shot from here, then move a little closer if the view is open.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the rows of pens with the grid so they look straight. Include some foreground, such as a rope of drying cloth, to give depth. For people, use the telephoto from a polite distance rather than walking up close.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a mid-tone area such as the wet concrete to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so bright cloth and sky do not wash out. Try a Live Photo for the movement of washing and hanging.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning, when the light is softer and the work is in full swing, tends to give the most comfortable photos.

text.access_note: This is a working laundry where people live and work, so be respectful and follow any local guidance on site.
claims_not_in_sources: Morning light is softer and gives more comfortable photos than harsh midday sun.
Photographing people at close range may be unwelcome, so it is polite to ask first.
Straight rows of pens look best when lined up with the phone's gridlines.
